list.listitem: Perform a thorough history and physical examination to determine the location, physical findings and symptoms associated with the mass. For some masses (e.g., umbilical hernia and bladder distension), examination findings may be definitive for diagnosis. C
For an upper quadrant mass with hematemesis, perform upper gastrointestinal endoscopy; if lower quadrant mass with hematochezia, perform colonoscopy. C
For a mass in the lower quadrants in woman of child-bearing age, perform transabdominal ultrasound (US) of the abdomen/pelvis. C

If the mass is suspicious for ovarian cancer, use transvaginal US as initial test, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) if ultrasound is unreliable and computed tomography (CT) if extra-ovarian disease is suspected. C
For a pulsatile midline mass, perform abdominal aortic ultrasound. C
If suspicion of diverticular or appendiceal abscess, order abdominal computed CT with IV, oral, and possible intra-luminal contrast. C

For most palpable abdominal masses suspected to be an intra-abdominal neoplasm in adults, the American College of Radiology (2019) recommends initial testing with either CT abdomen with IV contrast or ultrasound of the abdomen. For patients with a palpable abdominal mass suspected as being located in the abdominal wall, initial appropriate testing should be an US of the abdomen, CT abdomen with IV contrast, or MRI abdomen without and with IV contrast, each individually. C

background.definition: An abdominal mass is a palpable enlargement localized to the peritoneal cavity.

list.listitem: According to the National Center for Health Statistics (2015), the incidence of abdominal pain symptoms as the principle reason for the patient visit was 1.5% for office visits and 7.9% for emergency department visits.

The annual incidence of benign soft-tissue masses of the abdominal wall is estimated at 3,000 per million population. The rate of malignancy for those masses ranges from 5% to 42% based on case series.

Among patients with unexpected weight loss, the presence of an abdominal mass increases the likelihood of cancer and led to a revision of NICE recommendations for specialized investigation in men and women age 40 years and over with unexpected weight loss and an abdominal mass. In this study, using Clinical Practice Research Datalink electronic health records data linked to the National Cancer Registration in England, of 63,973 adults with unexpected weight loss, 908 (1.4%) had a diagnosis of cancer within six months of the index date. The presence of an abdominal mass increased the cancer risk from 2% or less (which falls below the 3% threshold for investigation) to 3.0% in those aged 40 to 60 years and 8.9% in those aged 60 to 80 years. Positive likelihood ratios for cancer in men ranged from 1.9 (95% CI, 1.3-2.6) for non-cardiac chest pain to 6.1 (3.4-10.8) for abdominal mass, and in women from 1.6 (1.1-2.3) for back pain to 21 (11-41) for jaundice.
See Differential Diagnosis table.
Unusual causes of abdominal mass include colonic tuberculosis, psoas abscess, and cesarean scar endometriosis.

The 3 most common abdominal malignancies in children are neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, and hepatoblastoma. Abdominal masses are also associated with certain genetic syndromes such renal cell carcinoma in patients with tuberous sclerosis or Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Additional information on syndromic abdominal malignancies can be found in the cited reference.

In a Chinese case series of cystic masses identified in 247 fetuses on prenatal ultrasound over a 2-year period, most were renal/adrenal cystic masses (37.7%), followed by hepatobiliary (19.4%), gastrointestinal (18.2%), reproductive system (11.7%), and ureter and bladder (10.9%) masses.
The palpable enlargement could be caused by increased amounts of air, fluid, or solid matter.

Air: Air is normally produced to a small degree in the colon. Large amounts of air production in the colon from bacterial fermentation could distend the colon, creating a palpable mass; or large amounts of swallowed air could distend the stomach to create a palpable mass. Bacterial growth with subsequent distention, bloating, pain, and can also occur in the stomach and/or small intestine (i.e., small intestinal bacterial overgrowth) and is believed to be due to retrograde movement of colonic bacteria. A perforation of the gastrointestinal tract will allow air to accumulate intraperitoneally, which could result in a palpable mass. Colonic retroperitoneal perforation from diverticulitis or locally advanced colon cancer can present as an air and pus collection for the former or a groin mass and psoas abscess in the latter.

Fluid: Increased fluid may accumulate in an abdominal organ as a result of blockage to normal fluid flow. A bladder distended with urine can result from prostatic hypertrophy and gall bladder distension can result from a bile duct blockage from a stone. A localized distension of a specific organ may present as an abdominal mass (cyst of the pancreas, liver, or kidney) and may result from either air or fluid accumulation in the cyst. Fluid can also present intraperitoneally in the form of ascites. Blood accumulation within an organ can present as an abdominal mass (splenic hematoma) or in the case of an enlarged abdominal aorta (aortic aneurysm). Although abscesses can be considered fluid, abscess formation is a defensive response usually to bacterial infection leading to a localized inflammatory response that leads to tissue damage. Abscesses contain inflammatory cells as well as necrotic tissue (pus), and may be caused by pathogens other than bacteria (e.g., parasites, fungi). Abscesses are typically walled off by a pseudocapsule which is a highly vascular and irregular inflammatory membrane.

Solid matter: An accumulation of solid matter such as feces within the colon can present as a mass (colonic fecal impaction). Leukemic infiltrate within the liver may present as a mass (hepatomegaly). Some solid abdominal masses result from herniation of the abdominal wall (ventral hernia and diastasis recti) or tumor.

list.listitem: When a palpable mass is detected on physical examination, the most important initial step is to attempt to define its general location in the abdomen: upper abdomen (above the umbilicus, either right or left), lower abdomen (below the umbilicus, either right or left), or midline.

If pain is a component of the abdominal mass, the location of the pain will be helpful in determining the anatomic location. As a general rule, the embryologic foregut structures such as the distal esophageus, stomach, duodenum, jejunum, spleen, liver, gall bladder, biliary tree, and pancreas will be located above the umbilicus and will have visceral pain referred to this area. The embryologic hindgut structures such as distal colon and anus will have pain as well as the anatomic mass below the umbilicus.
In a pre-menopausal woman with a lower abdominal mass, inquire about the last menstrual period, and if pregnancy is suspected, an ultrasound is needed.

Physical exam findings of an adnexal mass in a fertile woman in the absence of an intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound has a high likelihood ratio for ectopic pregnancy (LR+ 111; 95% CI, 12-1028). Additional findings that suggest ectopic pregnancy are cervical motion tenderness (LR+ 4.9; 95% CI, 1.7-14), an adnexal mass (LR+ 2.4; 95% CI, 1.6-3.7), and adnexal tenderness (LR+ 1.9; 95% CI, 1.0-3.5).

Physical exam findings, especially in an older woman, that increase the likelihood of an ovarian cancer include abdominal mass (LR+ 30.0), abdominal distension or increased girth (LR+ 16.0), abdominal or pelvic pain (LR+ 10.4) or bloating (LR+ 9.3), loss of appetite (LR+ 9.2), and family history of ovarian cancer (LR+ 7.5). However, no combination of symptoms was found to be useful as a screening tool in a low-prevalence population.

Inquiring about a history of gastrointestinal bleeding is the next step. Hematemesis in the presence of an upper abdominal mass suggests a potential intra-luminal intestinal lesion such as a malignancy of the stomach. Likewise, a lower abdominal mass in the presence of hematochezia suggests an intra-luminal colonic lesion.

The specific nature of the pain is important. Colic or recurrent crampy pain suggests biliary tract or intestinal obstruction. Looking for a ventral or umbilical hernia is important with bowel obstruction symptoms. With bowel obstruction, the 6 findings with the greatest sensitivity are distended abdomen, increased bowel sounds, history of constipation, previous abdominal surgery, age >50 years, and vomiting.

In upper quadrant masses with hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, the upper borders of the organs will not be palpated since they extend so far under the diaphragm. A distended gall bladder can sometimes be palpated on inspiration (Murphy's sign).

For midline masses, the consistency of the mass is important. A pulsatile mass on physical exam is fairly sensitive in detecting an aneurysm. Authors of a meta-analysis of 20 studies of ruptured aortic aneurysm including 2077 patients, however, found poor pooled sensitivities for both symptoms (abdominal pain, back pain, and syncope of 61.7%, 53.6%, and 27.8%, respectively) and signs (hypotension and pulsatile abdominal mass of 30.9% and 47.1%, respectively), based on low-certainty evidence. A suprapubic mass that is dull to percussion and disappears with insertion of a Foley catheter is a distended bladder.
For left lower quadrant tender masses with fever and change in bowel movements, think of diverticulitis in the older age group.

A right lower quadrant mass associated with appendicitis could be due to abscess or marked distension. Review to determine if the classic history is present: pain starting in the umbilical area and ending up at McBurney's point. Physical findings would include guarding and peritoneal inflammatory signs such as deep breathing exacerbating the pain.

Diagnostic testing for a palpable abdominal mass starts with localization of the mass (see algorithm in ). US is the first-line imaging modality for pregnant women and children where exposure to ionizing radiation from CT is of concern. In children, abdominal ultrasound Doppler imaging can also be useful for evaluating the vascular supply; if a tumor is identified, CT or MRI can be used to further characterize the mass and for staging.

If the patient is pre-menopausal and a menstrual history suggests pregnancy, an ultrasound (US) of the pelvis (transvaginal/transabdominal) is the test of choice by the American College of Radiology (ACR) Appropriateness Criteria. In the presence of hematochezia, the initial test is colonoscopy to detect an intra-luminal intestinal mass. In the presence of severe left lower quadrant pain with or without fever, with suspicion high for a mass of diverticulitis, the recommended test of choice is a CT scan of the abdomen with oral and IV contrast or MRI without and with contrast. CT is also optimal in identifying other inflammatory lower quadrant masses such as appendicitis.

Although comparative studies in the evaluation of palpable masses with MRI versus CT or US are not available, MRI has advantages for evaluating complex lesions not well characterized by US or CT and is particularly useful for characterizing fat, protein, fluid, blood products, vascularized tissue, and metal (ACR). Additionally, MRI does not entail exposure to ionizing radiation.

If an adnexal cyst is suspected, this can be diagnosed and followed by transvaginal ultrasound. In women with an adnexal mass suspicious of ovarian cancer, the Program in Evidence-based Care recommends transvaginal US as the initial test, MRI if ultrasound is unreliable, and CT if extra-ovarian disease is suspected; a cancer antigen 125 test may help differentiate between a benign and potentially malignant mass, but should not be used alone.

Bowel endometriosis, affecting between 3.8% and 37% of women with endometriosis, can present as a lower quadrant mass. If the diagnosis can’t be made empirically or on transvaginal ultrasound, direct visualization using laparoscopy may be needed. Endometriosis can also occur in the abdominal wall; in one case series, most cases were secondary to obstetric or gynecological surgeries and located in umbilical or Cesarean section scars possibly related to iatrogenic transfer of the endometrial tissue.

In the presence of hematemesis, an upper GI endoscopy is the test of choice to identify the potential intra-luminal intestinal mass. With right upper quadrant pain and suspicion of biliary obstruction by history, it is important to order either a sonogram or CT of the biliary tree to confirm the location of the obstruction. If a focal palpable mass is suspected in the liver, order an MRI. For detection of other palpable abdominal masses, CT of the abdomen is recommended.

If the mass is pulsatile with suspicion for an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), the imaging study of choice is ultrasound of the aorta. Emergency bedside ultrasonography has a high sensitivity and specificity for detecting an AAA in symptomatic patients in the emergency department. For better definition of the anatomy of the aorta and its branches, CT angiography is recommended. In the meta-analysis cited above, CT angiography had a pooled sensitivity of 91% and specificity of 94% for diagnosis of ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (LR+ 15, LR- .09).

A midline hernia can be diagnosed by physical exam listening for bowel sounds and checking to see if it can be reduced. A distended bladder will lie in the suprapubic area; the mass will disappear with the passage of a Foley catheter into the bladder.

Endoscopic ultrasound-guided (EUS) tissue acquisition using either fine needle aspiration (FNA) or needle core biopsy has become a mainstay for tissue diagnosis of abdominal mass lesions. Authors of a prospective study including 58 patients with a solid intra-abdominal mass who underwent both procedures found the two comparable with respect to diagnostic accuracy, sample adequacy, number of passes and safety, with fine-needle biopsy preferred in select cases where maintained tissue architecture is needed. Use of conventional cytology and cell block preparation may increase diagnostic accuracy of EUS-FNA compared to either method alone.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 12 studies including 7 RCTs of EUS-FNA compared to EUS-FNB (fine needle biopsy) for solid pancreatic mass lesions found EUS-FNB had higher diagnostic accuracy and specimen adequacy using fewer needle passes than EUS-FNA. Rates of overall complications and technical failures were similar.

Macroscopic on-site evaluation (MOSE) of the tissue specimen obtained during endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration/biopsy, with additional needle passes if needed, increased sensitivity and cytopathology diagnostic yield in one prospective study. Post-procedural adverse events occurred in 33 patients (3.3%). In one RCT including 96 consecutive patients undergoing EUS fine needle aspiration for solid lesions, use of MOSE resulted in high and comparable diagnostic accuracy (95.8% in conventional vs 91.6% in MOSE arm) with fewer passes. In a single institution retrospective study of cases involving solid pancreatic lesions, use of rapid on-site evaluation significantly improved diagnostic accuracy for EUS-FNA but did not for cases using EUS-FNB.

Congenital disorders associated with abdominal masses include enteric duplication cysts that can occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract, subdiaphragmatic extra-lobar pulmonary sequestration which consists of malformed pulmonary parenchyma, and kidney disorders including hydronephrosis, ureteropelvic or ureterovesical junction obstruction, multicystic dysplastic kidney, and autosomal-recessive polycystic kidney disease.

For suspected neuroblastoma, nuclear medicine metaiodobenzyl-guanidine (MIBG) imaging is also indicated at initial staging because 90% of neuroblastoma tumors demonstrate MIBG avidity; fluorodeoxyglucose/positron emission tomography (FDG/PET) may be useful for tumors lacking MIBG avidity.
For patients with Wilms tumor, chest CT with contrast is indicated for diagnosing pulmonary metastatic disease.

For patients with suspected hepatoblastoma on US, authors of one review prefer MRI over CT for staging due to its superior contrast resolution, use of hepatobiliary-specific contrast agents, and potential for multiphase, dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging without radiation exposure.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to diagnosis.
The differential diagnosis of abdominal masses is extensive. The location of the mass is a good starting point for the differential diagnosis.

Confirming the presence of a mass through imaging should be the first step in the workup following the clinical evaluation; the percentages of patients with suspected abdominal mass who had a diagnosis corroborated by imaging range from 16% to 68.3% (ACR).

The American College of Radiology (ACR, 2019) state that the tests that are usually appropriate for initial imaging of a palpable abdominal mass suspected to be an intra-abdominal neoplasm in adults are US of the abdomen or CT abdomen with IV contrast, individually. These procedures are viewed as equivalent alternatives. When US findings are indeterminate, CT imaging should be obtained in a timely manner. Tests that may be appropriate include MRI abdomen without and with IV contrast, CT abdomen without IV contrast, and MRI abdomen without IV contrast. MRI has the advantage of very high soft-tissue contrast allowing depiction and differentiation of cystic structures, soft-tissue components, fat, and blood products and IV contrast improves visualization of normal organs and pathology; however, there are no comparative studies of use of MRI in this setting. Recommendations are based on limited data on undifferentiated masses; most studies from case series and occurring in the 1980s. These studies are reviewed on the ACR website.

For patients with a palpable abdominal mass suspected as being located in the abdominal wall, initial appropriate testing should be an US of the abdomen, CT abdomen with IV contrast, or MRI abdomen without and with IV contrast, each individually (ACR, 2019). These procedures are also seen as equivalent alternatives. Tests that may be appropriate are MRI abdomen without IV contrast, CT abdomen without IV contrast.
